{{Short description|Class of natural numbers with many divisors}}
[[Image:Divisor.svg|thumb|right|Divisor function {{math|''d''(''n'')}} up to {{math|1=''n'' = 250}}]]
[[Image:Prime powers in SHCN, CAN.svg|thumb|right|Prime-power factors]]

In [[number theory]], a '''superior highly composite number''' is a [[natural number]] which, in a particular rigorous sense, has many [[divisors]]. Particularly, it is defined by a [[ratio]] between the number of divisors an [[integer]] has and that integer raised to some positive power.

For any possible [[Exponentiation|exponent]], whichever integer has the greatest ratio is a superior highly composite number. It is a stronger restriction than that of a [[highly composite number]], which is defined as having more divisors than any smaller positive integer.

The first ten superior highly composite numbers and their factorization are listed.

[[File:Highly composite numbers.svg|thumb|250px|Plot of the number of divisors of integers from 1 to 1000. Highly composite numbers are labelled in bold and superior highly composite numbers are starred. In the [http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Highly_composite_numbers.svg SVG file], hover over a bar to see its statistics.]]

For a superior highly composite number {{mvar|n}} there exists a positive real number {{math|''ε'' > 0}} such that for all natural numbers {{math|''k'' > 1}} we have <math display="block">\frac{d(n)}{n^\varepsilon}\geq\frac{d(k)}{k^\varepsilon}</math> where {{math|''d''(''n'')}}, the [[divisor function]], denotes the number of divisors of {{mvar|n}}. The term was coined by [[Ramanujan]] (1915).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Superior Highly Composite Number |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SuperiorHighlyCompositeNumber.html |access-date=2021-03-05 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

For example, the number with the most divisors per square root of the number itself is 12; this can be demonstrated using some highly composites near 12.
<math display="block">\frac{2}{2^{0.5}}\approx 1.414, \frac{3}{4^{0.5}}=1.5, \frac{4}{6^{0.5}}\approx 1.633, \frac{6}{12^{0.5}}\approx 1.732, \frac{8}{24^{0.5}}\approx 1.633, \frac{12}{60^{0.5}}\approx 1.549</math>

120 is another superior highly composite number because it has the highest ratio of divisors to itself raised to the 0.4 power.
<math display="block">\frac{9}{36^{0.4}}\approx 2.146, \frac{10}{48^{0.4}}\approx 2.126, \frac{12}{60^{0.4}}\approx 2.333, \frac{16}{120^{0.4}}\approx 2.357, \frac{18}{180^{0.4}}\approx 2.255, \frac{20}{240^{0.4}}\approx 2.233, \frac{24}{360^{0.4}}\approx 2.279</math>

The first 15 superior highly composite numbers, [[2 (number)|2]], [[6 (number)|6]], [[12 (number)|12]], [[60 (number)|60]], [[120 (number)|120]], [[360 (number)|360]], [[2520 (number)|2520]], [[5040 (number)|5040]], 55440, 720720, 1441440, 4324320, 21621600, 367567200, 6983776800 {{OEIS|id=A002201}} are also the first 15 [[Colossally abundant number|colossally abundant numbers]], which meet a similar condition based on the sum-of-divisors function rather than the number of divisors. Neither set, however, is a subset of the other.

== Properties ==
{{Euler diagram numbers with many divisors.svg}}
All superior highly composite numbers are [[Highly composite number|highly composite]]. This is easy to prove: if there is some number ''k'' that has the same number of divisors as ''n'' but is less than ''n'' itself (i.e. <math>d(k) = d(n)</math>, but <math>k<n</math>), then <math>\frac{d(k)}{k^\varepsilon} > \frac{d(n)}{n^\varepsilon}</math> for all positive ε, so if a number "n" is not highly composite, it cannot be superior highly composite. Furthermore, all superior highly numbers have the greatest possible number of divisors for the number of (not necessarily distinct) prime factors it has.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-02-21 |title=Dozensonline-Oddcompoflanks |url=https://www.tapatalk.com/groups/dozensonline/oddcompoflanks-t546.html |access-date=2025-12-04 |website=Dozensonline |language=en-gb}}</ref>

An effective construction of the set of all superior highly composite numbers is given by the following monotonic mapping from the positive real numbers.<ref>Ramanujan (1915); see also URL http://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/hcn.dvi</ref> Let
<math display="block">e_p(x) = \left\lfloor \frac{1}{\sqrt[x]{p} - 1} \right\rfloor</math>
for any prime number ''p'' and positive real ''x''. Then
<math display="block">s(x) = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{e_p(x)}</math> is a superior highly composite number.

Note that the product need not be computed indefinitely, because if <math>p > 2^x</math> then <math>e_p(x) = 0</math>, so the product to calculate <math>s(x)</math> can be terminated once <math>p \ge 2^x</math>.

Also note that in the definition of <math>e_p(x)</math>, <math>1/x</math> is analogous to <math>\varepsilon</math> in the implicit definition of a superior highly composite number.

Moreover, for each superior highly composite number <math>s'</math> exists a half-open interval <math>I \subset \R^+</math> such that <math>\forall x \in I: s(x) = s'</math>.

This representation implies that there exist an infinite sequence of <math>\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots \in \mathbb{P}</math> such that for the ''n''-th superior highly composite number <math>s_n</math> holds
<math display="block">s_n = \prod_{i=1}^n \pi_i</math>

The first <math>\pi_i</math> are 2, 3, 2, 5, 2, 3, 7, ... {{OEIS|id=A000705}}.  In other words, the quotient of two successive superior highly composite numbers is a prime number.

== Radices ==
The first few superior highly composite numbers have often been used as [[Radix|radices]], due to their high divisibility for their size. For example:
* [[Binary number|Binary]] (base 2)
* [[Senary]] (base 6)
* [[Duodecimal]] (base 12)
* [[Sexagesimal]] (base 60)

Bigger SHCNs can be used in other ways. 120 appears as the [[long hundred]], while 360 appears as the number of [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] in a circle.
